What the network shows

Results from the same 666-district network used in the simulator above. Each figure from the report is shown next to its numbers.

01 · Topology

A near-planar lattice, not a scale-free network

0

0
border edges
0

0
clustering

Most districts have five or six neighbours and there is no heavy tail, so the network looks like a planar lattice, not a scale-free graph. Clustering is 0.463, much higher than a random graph of the same density, which is what you would expect from geography.

02 · Chokepoint

The Siliguri Corridor is the network's chokepoint

0
Darjeeling
0
Jalpaiguri
0
Koch Bihar
0
Uttar Dinajpur

These four districts in northern West Bengal have the highest betweenness in the country, 40 to 65 percent above any other region. They are the only land link to the seven northeastern states (about 45 million people), so removing them cuts the northeast off from the rest of the network.

03 · Arrival time

Central districts got their first case earlier

Across the 517 districts with both arrival time and centrality, closeness is the best predictor of how early the first case showed up. All four correlations are negative, but they are small, so network position only explains part of it.

04 · Communities

Communities follow geography rather than state lines

0
Louvain communities

Louvain finds 13 clusters whose boundaries follow rivers, corridors and mountain ranges, and they often cross state lines. The network's natural neighbourhoods do not line up with state borders.

05 · Case burden

Where the cases were

0 / 666
districts with case data

Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh had the most confirmed cases, mostly around big cities and dense populations. 522 of 666 districts have case data. The rest stay in the network so connectivity is not affected.
